sections.h2: Where the land records are kept
sections.html:
The Recorder's staff work from Suite 100 on the ground level of the courthouse annex, 1 West Liberty Street, Farmington. The county suggests using the rear main parking lot entrance. The office records, maintains and archives deeds, liens, marriage licenses, surveys, plats and military discharge papers.

  • Phone: 573-756-2323, or 573-431-6505 then option 1 and 7.
  • Hours: weekdays, 8:00 a.m. until 4:00 p.m.
  • Cards: debit and credit are taken, with a convenience fee of at least $2.00 on each transaction.
  • Search: the deed index books and all recorded documents are online in Tapestry under Land Records Search. A Laredo subscription is another option, so ask the office.

This office also records federal and state tax liens and their releases, and you can ask for copies by letter or at the counter. Down the hall are the Assessor (Suite 200) and the Collector (Suite 201), which makes a single visit enough for a lien check, a parcel record and a tax payoff ahead of a sale.

Recording fees come from RSMo 59.310. Senate Bill 938 added a flat $2.00 statewide increase for documents, marriage licenses and plats or surveys. Call for the all-in total for your page count before you drive over.

Common Recorder charges in Farmington
Recording serviceFee
Recording a deed or instrument$5 first page, $3 each additional page (before the $2 increase)
Document that does not meet format rules$25 added to the normal fees
Release or assignment of more than one item$5 per item beyond the first
Copy of a recorded instrumentUp to $2 first page, $1 each additional
Certificate and seal outside a recording$1
Copy of a federal or state tax lien or release$1.00 per page

If you wonder whether a transfer-related charge applies to your deed, ask the Recorder at 573-756-2323.

RSMo 59.310 lets the Recorder refuse a paper that ignores the layout rules, or accept it with a $25 surcharge. If it is refused, the reason must be given in writing. Even certified court copies must include the property's legal description.

  • Paper: letter size, white or pale, 20 pound stock, printed on one side, with no attachments stapled on unless a statute demands them.
  • Margins: three blank inches across the top of page one for the Recorder, and at least 3/4 inch elsewhere.
  • Type: eight point or larger, in black or dark ink, sharp enough to copy cleanly.
  • Signatures: dark ink, each with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped below.

Under that margin the first page lists the title, the date, every grantor (labeled Grantor, with marital status), every grantee (labeled Grantee), any addresses a statute requires, the legal description and book and page references if they apply. A cover sheet can hold the same details. Some papers skip the format rules altogether: anything signed before January 1, 2002, military separation papers, documents executed outside the United States and court judgments.

sections.h2: What if a recorded deed has an error?
sections.html:
It can be re-recorded, but the second filing faces the same tests as a fresh one. The county wants correct margins, legibility and first page information, a new cover sheet saying why the document is being recorded again, and a new acknowledgment from the notary.

With a closing around the corner, a mistake can hold up the title company. It takes only a wrong legal description or a grantor's name left off. Ask the escrow officer to check the deed before signing. Owners can also sign up for the Recorder's free Property Fraud Alert, which sends a warning if someone records a fake document claiming your home. Subscribe online or phone 800-728-3858.

St. Francois County is part of Missouri's Lead Belt, with Farmington as seat and biggest city. It counts roughly 67,809 residents in 29,596 homes, and owners hold 68.2% of households. Median home value is $169,300, median rent $794 and median household income $57,477. Five school districts serve it: Bismarck R-V, Farmington R-VII, North St. Francois County R-1, St. Francois County Central R-III and West St. Francois County R-IV.

sections.h2: Property tax, tax sale and installment plan
sections.html:
Suite 201 houses the Collector (573-756-2645), who handles both current and past-due tax and holds the county tax sale on the fourth Monday of August. Parcels still owing after June 30 can be redeemed only by paying in full with cash, a money order or a cashier's check, up to 4:00 p.m. on the Friday before the sale. The Assessor's number is 573-756-1878, in Suite 200.

Pay at the Collector's office or online. December 31 is the last day each year to pay without late charges. Owners whose taxes are not paid through a mortgage escrow can use an installment plan run with EquaPay. The county describes four steps: look up your bill, create an account and pick a draft date and method (bank account or card), let EquaPay calculate payments from the time left before the due date, and finish enrollment so it pays the county on time.

sections.h2: Senior tax credit and your buyer
sections.html:
A senior tax credit belongs to the qualifying taxpayer's homestead and cannot be handed to the next owner or carried to another house. Someone who moves and still qualifies applies again, and the new address gets its own base year.

Enrollment runs March 1 through May 31, in person at the Collector's office between 9:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m., with photo ID. Applicants must be 62 by January 1 of the base year and current on tax. Review can take up to 30 days, and both spouses on the deed are asked to apply in person. Trust or LLC owners must bring their documents.

The credit equals the difference between this year's tax on the homestead and the base-year tax. Assessed value is not frozen, so the credit can change, and by law the State Blind Pension Fund and voter-approved bond levies stay outside it. Delinquent tax disqualifies an applicant. If you are selling, expect the buyer's first bill to differ from yours, and ask the Collector (573-756-2645) what applies to the parcel.

sections.h2: Recording a deed when you sell
sections.html:
Typically the title company or closing attorney drafts the deed, gets it signed and notarized, and files it with the Recorder once the sale closes. You should read the legal description and both parties' names before signing, because a typo there often leads to a second filing. Hang on to the stamped copy as evidence the deed made it onto the record.

A cash sale goes the same way. You skip the wait for a buyer's loan, yet the deed meets identical format rules and fees, so find out from the closing agent who pays them.

faqs.q: How do I search for a recorded deed?
faqs.a: Use the Land Records Search tab on the Recorder's page, which opens Tapestry and shows the deed index books and recorded documents. You can also call 573-756-2323 or visit the annex in Farmington.

faqs.q: When can I visit the Recorder?
faqs.a: The doors are open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Holiday closings are posted on the county website's office closures page.

faqs.q: Why might my deed come back unrecorded?
faqs.a: The usual causes are a missing legal description, a first page without the three-inch top margin, text smaller than eight point or missing grantor and grantee labels. The office must return a rejected document with the reason.
Yes. The office takes debit and credit cards and charges a minimum $2.00 convenience fee on every transaction.

faqs.q: Is property tax paid to the Recorder?
faqs.a: No. The Collector bills and collects property tax at Suite 201 of the same annex building. The Recorder handles deeds, liens and plats.
